name: Blue-Green and Rolling Deployments
intent: Replace running servers with a new version without downtime, either a few at a time (rolling) or by building a full second environment and switching traffic to it (blue-green).
scenario: A web tier of 6 servers runs v1 and serves about 500 requests per second; each server handles 100, so 5 healthy servers is the minimum. The team ships v2 first with a rolling update, then with a blue-green switch.
problem: Stopping all the servers and starting the new version causes downtime. Replacing them carelessly can be just as bad: take too many out at once and the rest are overloaded, kill a server mid-request and users see errors, send traffic to a server that is still booting and it fails. And if v2 turns out to be broken, you need to get back to v1 fast.

howItWorks.title: Rolling: replace in batches, bounded by two numbers
howItWorks.text: A controller replaces servers a few at a time. Max surge says how many extra servers may exist above the desired count (for example 6 plus 1). Max unavailable says how many may be missing from the ready count. With surge 1 and unavailable 0 it starts a new server first and only removes an old one once the new one is ready, so capacity never dips. With surge 0 and unavailable 1 it needs no spare hardware but runs one server short. Both at 0 can never make progress.

howItWorks.title: Readiness and draining protect users
howItWorks.text: A new server only receives traffic after its readiness check passes (the app has booted, warmed caches and can reach the database), so the delay before it is ready sets the pace of the whole rollout. An old server is first taken out of the load balancer, then given a draining period (often 30 to 60 seconds) to finish in-flight requests, and only then stopped. Skip draining and those requests fail.

howItWorks.title: Mixed versions run together
howItWorks.text: For the length of a rolling update, v1 and v2 both serve live traffic and share the same database, cache and message formats. The two versions must therefore be compatible with each other: no breaking API changes, no schema the old code cannot read. This is the main design constraint of a rolling update.

howItWorks.title: Blue-green: a whole second environment and one switch
howItWorks.text: Blue is the live environment (v1). You build green, a full-size copy running v2, and test it with no user traffic. When it is healthy, you flip the router, load balancer or DNS record so all traffic goes to green. Blue is kept running for a while as the rollback target, then shut down. There is no mixed-version window at the servers: users see v1 or v2, never both.

howItWorks.title: Rollback: instant versus replayed
howItWorks.text: In blue-green, rollback is flipping the router back, which takes seconds as long as blue is still up. In a rolling update, rollback is another rolling update in the opposite direction (v2 to v1), which takes as long as the first one did, and the broken version keeps serving some users while it runs.

howItWorks.title: The database is shared, so change it in two phases
howItWorks.text: Both strategies usually point v1 and v2 at the same database. Use expand/contract: first expand (add the new column or table, keep the old one, write both), deploy v2 which reads the new shape, and only contract (drop the old column) once v1 is gone and a rollback is no longer wanted. A single step that renames or drops a column breaks whichever version is still running.

pros: No downtime when done correctly: capacity stays at or above demand throughout
Rolling needs little or no spare capacity (max surge 0 or 1) and is the default in most orchestrators
Rolling limits the damage of a bug to the share of servers already replaced
Blue-green gives a clean cut-over, a full pre-switch test of the real environment, and a rollback of seconds
Blue-green has no mixed-version window between servers
cons: Rolling runs two versions at once, so every change must be backward compatible, and bugs that only appear in mixed state are hard to reproduce
Rolling rollback is slow: it is a second full rollout, during which the bad version is still serving
Blue-green doubles the server cost while both environments exist (12 servers instead of 6 in this example)
Blue-green sends 100% of traffic to v2 at once, so a bug the tests missed hits every user until you flip back
Neither strategy solves database changes by itself; that needs expand/contract and discipline
whenToUse: Rolling: stateless services behind a load balancer, where v1 and v2 are compatible and spare capacity is limited
Blue-green: releases that must switch at one moment (incompatible API versions, big framework upgrades) or where a very fast rollback is worth the extra cost
Either: any service where downtime during a release is not acceptable
whenNotToUse: Blue-green for large stateful fleets, where cloning the whole environment (data included) is too slow or expensive
Rolling when v1 and v2 cannot coexist and you cannot make them compatible
Either as a substitute for canary releases when you want to measure v2 on a small slice of real traffic before committing
Either for a hobby app with a maintenance window: a restart at 3 a.m. is simpler and cheaper
pitfalls: A readiness check that only says the process is up: traffic arrives before caches are warm or the database connection works, and the rollout spreads a broken version
Max unavailable set so high that the remaining servers are overloaded; check it against peak load, not average load
No connection draining or a termination timeout shorter than your longest request, so in-flight requests are cut off
Dropping or renaming a database column in the same release that stops using it: the still-running version breaks, and rollback is impossible
Switching blue-green and shutting blue down immediately, so the rollback you paid for is gone
Warm-up forgotten: green has cold caches and connection pools, so the first minutes after the switch are slow; send it a trickle or replay traffic first
Sticky sessions or long-lived connections (WebSockets) that keep clients on the old version long after the switch

roles.label: Load balancer / router
roles.description: Sends each request to a ready server, and is what you change to drain a server or switch environments.

roles.label: Old version (v1)
roles.description: The servers running the current release; they are drained and retired, or kept as the rollback target.

roles.label: New version (v2)
roles.description: The servers running the new release, brought up and checked for readiness before they get traffic.

roles.label: Shared database
roles.description: Used by both versions at the same time, so its schema must work for v1 and v2.

quiz.question: A web tier has 6 servers that each handle 100 requests per second. Peak traffic is 550 requests per second, so all 6 must be serving at peak. You roll out v2 with a rolling update during peak. Which setting keeps capacity from dipping?
options: Max surge 0 and max unavailable 1, so only one server is out at a time and the dip is small.
Max surge 1 and max unavailable 0, so a new server is ready before an old one is removed.
Max surge 0 and max unavailable 2, so the rollout finishes quickly and the dip is short.
Max surge 1 and max unavailable 1, so the rollout moves fast and a spare covers the removed server.
quiz.explanation: With 550 requests per second you cannot lose even one ready server, so unavailable must be 0 and the extra server must come from surge. The other settings allow 5 or 4 ready servers, which cannot carry the load.

quiz.question: v2 of an app stops using the column phone and reads a new column mobile instead. The team plans a blue-green release and wants to rename the column in one migration just before the switch, since users never see a mix of versions. What is the best approach?
options: Run the rename just before the switch, because blue-green avoids mixed versions and so avoids the problem.
Rename the column as soon as green passes its checks, so blue keeps working with the old name through a database view or alias.
Run the rename in the first minutes after the switch, when little traffic has reached the new environment.
Add mobile and write to both columns, switch to v2, and drop phone in a later release once rollback is no longer wanted.
quiz.explanation: Blue and green share one database, so a rename breaks whichever version is not expecting it and removes your rollback. Expand then contract keeps both versions working.

quiz.question: A team flips traffic from blue (v1) to green (v2) at 14:00 and shuts blue down at 14:05 to save money. At 14:40 a bug that only hits real data is found in v2. What is their position?
options: They have lost the instant rollback, and must redeploy v1 as a new release, which takes about as long as a normal deploy.
They can flip the router back in seconds, because the switch is a routing change and not a deployment.
They can roll back in seconds, because the green environment can be pointed at the v1 image.
They are fine, because rollback in a blue-green setup works for any time after the switch.
quiz.explanation: Blue-green rollback is only fast while the old environment is still running. Once blue is gone, going back is a fresh deployment, which is the cost of removing the safety net too early.
